text:
Sweet Corn.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Sweet corn needs an early variety suited to local summers and a warm, sunny, sheltered site. Full-sized cobs need wind pollination: plant a block of short rows. Expect one main cob per plant, sometimes a smaller second. Baby corn is picked before pollination and can grow in rows.

Quick facts
Sow indoors

Mid-Apr in cool districts.

Harvest

Aug – Oct

Germination

10–12 days

Sowing depth

1 in.

Row spacing

Between rows: 16 in.; arrange full-sized corn in a block

Yield (10 ft row)

About 10 cobs from this row length within a block

Plant spacing

Full-sized cobs: 16 in. each way; baby corn: plants 8 in. apart

Ready in

About 10–16 weeks from sowing for early varieties; later varieties take longer

Sow

Outdoors from mid-May in warm soil. Later than mid-Jun, only quick varieties or baby corn.

Plant out

Late May–Jun after hardening off.

Recommended varieties
SUPERSWEET
Swift F1

Early, compact corn with tender, sweet kernels for short UK summers.

SUPERSWEET
Earlibird F1

Early supersweet hybrid for ripe cobs in comparatively short summers.

TENDERSWEET
Lark F1

Mid-season tendersweet with soft, sweet kernels, extending early harvests.

BABY CORN
Minipop F1

Baby corn: pick small, immature cobs; a separate use from full-sized sweetcorn.

Key risks
Slugs

Slugs damage young plants most when cold or wet conditions slow growth.

Cold check

Cold soil and weather slow growth and nutrient uptake; seedlings may turn yellow and stall.

Poor pollination

Gaps in full-sized cobs commonly result from poor pollination.

Cross pollination

Pollen from maize or different sweet-corn types can reduce the sweetness or tenderness of supersweet cobs.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
90
FRUITING CROPS

Plant full-sized corn in a block.

Pollen must reach the silks. Baby corn is picked before pollination and can grow in rows.

Keep plants warm and well watered.

Moisture matters especially during flowering and cob filling.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, humus-rich soil with rotted compost: moist, warm and well drained.
Choose a sunny, sheltered site and neutral to slightly acid soil. In cool areas, prioritise warmth and drainage.
Sowing & planting
Raise and plant
Block for full cobs
Sow 

Place one or two seeds in each pot or spot. Keep the stronger seedling. Use pots for an early start or sow in the final bed when the soil is warm.

Plant out 

Harden off and plant with the rootball intact. Water in. For full-sized cobs, make a block of at least four short rows so pollen reaches the silks. Baby corn can grow in rows because the cobs are picked before pollination.

Looking after the crop
Weed while plants are small, avoiding the spreading roots. Mulch and water during dry weather, particularly as tassels shed pollen and cobs swell.
Cover exposed basal roots lightly with soil or compost and leave side shoots. Tap shedding tassels to help full-cob pollination; baby corn needs none.
Harvesting & storage
As silks brown, test a kernel. Milky juice means the cob is ready, clear juice is too early and doughy kernels are past their best. Check often.
Twist cobs off carefully and use promptly. Check for smaller second cobs; pick baby corn while young, with silks still white.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Young plants are chewed in cool weather.	Raise sturdy plants; inspect and hand-pick around seedlings.
Cold check	Young plants yellow and stop growing.	Wait for warm soil; harden off and protect early crops.
Poor pollination	Cobs have gaps or poorly filled kernels.	Plant blocks, water well and tap shedding tassels.
Cross pollination	Supersweet eating quality is reduced.	Isolate corn types as the seed packet advises.
Birds	Ripe kernels are pecked.	Protect ripening cobs with secure covers or taut netting.
Badgers	Plants flattened; cobs eaten near ripeness.	Fit suitable crop barriers before cobs ripen.
Smut	Large swollen galls appear on cobs or stems.	Remove affected growth before galls burst; rotate.
Frit fly	Ragged leaves on stunted seedlings.	Sow into warm soil to keep seedlings growing.
Final tips

Check variety isolation advice: nearby maize or different sweet-corn types can affect eating quality.

Chop healthy spent stems for compost; tough pieces may need a second composting cycle.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
91
FRUITING CROPS
